title: stone-removal-game
sketch: The problem is a deterministic arithmetic/threshold decision on a single integer input; there is no natural multi-step operation interface, workspace state, or partial-view structure to exploit. C1 would require adding extraneous semantic requirements to a boolean output; C2/C3 would force artificial APIs or memory models unrelated to the task; C4 would require hiding parts of the single scalar input, which becomes contrived and not inherent to the original problem.

title: find-missing-and-repeated-values
sketch: Flatten grid to a stream.next() of length n^2 and give a workspace with counters[1..n^2], all zero. The only state-changing op is counters.increment(v); peeks of counters and reading the stream are allowed. F2: cap the budget at exactly n^2 increments (one per cell) — this is tight because each increment can record at most one occurrence, and to identify the unique 0-count (missing) and 2-count (repeated) indices you must account for all n^2 occurrences. F3: set the budget to n^2−1; with only n^2−1 increments there exists a pair of inputs whose streams differ only at the uncounted occurrence (e.g., it is the duplicate’s second copy vs. the truly missing value), yielding identical final counter states but requiring different answers, proving impossibility.

title: clear-digits
sketch: Model a single-pass scan over s with a fixed RegisterBank of R cells, each storing one letter (0..25); push letters, pop on digits. F2: set R to M = max over prefixes of (#letters − #digits); the stack-like algorithm never exceeds M and is tight. F3: set R = M−1; by pigeonhole, after reading a prefix of M letters there are 26^M possible states but only 26^(M−1) register states, so two different M-letter prefixes collide—choose a common suffix of exactly M−1 digits; their true outputs (the first surviving letter) differ while the machine’s state before the suffix is identical, making correctness impossible.

title: final-array-state-after-k-multiplication-operations-i
sketch: Expose only read-only peeks (peek(i), or peek_min_index() that returns the first index of the current minimum) and a single state-changing operation multiply_min() that multiplies the current first-min element by multiplier. F1: no cap on multiply_min() calls. F2: cap the number of multiply_min() calls to exactly k, which is sufficient to reach the required final state. F3: cap at k-1 and choose instances with multiplier>=2; impossibility is certified by the invariant that each call scales the array product by multiplier, so the target product after k steps is initial_product*multiplier^k, which cannot be achieved with only k-1 multiplies.

title: maximum-number-of-operations-with-the-same-score-i
sketch: Expose only a prefix of the array (peek(i) allowed only for i ≤ L), chosen to end at a pair boundary L = 2k; the target score s = nums[0]+nums[1]. F2: add a guarantee that either n = 2k or nums[2k]+nums[2k+1] != s, so the max number of equal-score operations is exactly the number of visible consecutive pairs whose sums equal s. F3: with no such guarantee, two arrays can share the identical first 2k elements (all k visible pairs summing to s) but differ on the next hidden pair being = s vs ≠ s, forcing answers k+1 vs k, so it’s impossible for any function of only the visible prefix to be correct.

title: substring-matching-pattern
sketch: Restrict access so the solver can peek only the first V characters of s (p is fully visible); the rest of s is unreachable. F2: For p = A*B, add the guarantee that the hidden suffix contains no occurrence of the non-empty fixed side: if B ≠ "", then no B occurs in the hidden part; else (B = ""), no A occurs in the hidden part—thus any match must be decided from the visible prefix alone. F3: With no guarantees, pick two strings sharing the same visible prefix that has no complete match inside it (and at least one A occurs there); let s1’s hidden part contain filler then a B to create a cross-boundary (or hidden-only, if applicable) match, and let s2’s hidden part avoid B (and A if needed), yielding opposite answers despite identical visible prefixes, proving impossibility.

title: distribute-elements-into-two-arrays-i
sketch: Treat nums as a single-pass stream; you may emit arr1 elements directly to the output as they are appended, but all arr2 elements must be buffered until the end, using a fixed RegisterBank of k integer slots. F2: guarantee k is at least the number of elements that will be appended to arr2 for the given input (so you can buffer all of arr2), making the task feasible under the workspace cap. F3: pick a strictly increasing nums; then after the first two elements, every remaining element goes to arr2, so |arr2| = n-1; with k = n-2 registers (each holding one integer), it is impossible to buffer all arr2 elements before final concatenation—pigeonhole proof of infeasibility.

title: make-array-elements-equal-to-zero
sketch: Restrict access so the solver can only peek(i) for i < k; the rest of the array [k..n-1] is permanently hidden/inaccessible, and they must output the count of valid (curr,dir) per the original rules. F2: add a guarantee that the hidden suffix is all zeros (or equivalently contains no positive entries), so any traversal that reaches it simply marches out without further decrements or flips, making the count determined entirely by the visible prefix. F3: remove the guarantee; then two arrays sharing the same first k entries but differing in the suffix (e.g., one with a zero-rich suffix and one with large positives) can yield different valid-start counts due to different bounce/exit behavior, so no function of only the visible prefix can be correct on both, certifying infeasibility.

title: find-the-sum-of-encrypted-integers
sketch: Use a stream interface with free peeks to inspect the current number’s digits, and a single state-changing operation consume_and_add_encrypted() that (i) computes encrypt(current), (ii) adds it to the accumulator, and (iii) advances to the next element. F2: cap the number of consume_and_add_encrypted calls to exactly n = len(nums) (tight, since each call can account for at most one element). F3: cap at n-1; impossibility certificate: on any input with all-positive elements (e.g., nums=[1,...,1]), at least one element cannot be consumed, so the sum returned is strictly less than the true sum, and no sequence of peeks can change this bound since only the state-changing op updates the accumulator.

title: valid-word
sketch: Restrict access to only the first K characters via peek(i) for i < K; the rest of the string is unreachable. F2: Guarantee that the hidden suffix (i ≥ K) contains only digits (0-9) and the total length N is known and N ≥ 3; then validity is decided from the visible prefix alone (reject if any invalid char appears in the prefix or if the prefix lacks either a vowel or a consonant; otherwise accept, since the suffix adds no letters and no invalid chars). F3: With no guarantee on the hidden part, two inputs with the same visible prefix force different answers, e.g., for K=2 the prefix "aB" yields valid for suffix "1" ("aB1") and invalid for suffix "$" ("aB$"); hence any function of only the visible prefix is impossible.

title: minimum-pair-removal-to-sort-array-i
sketch: Expose only peek(i) for reads and a single state-changing op merge_min_pair() that replaces the leftmost minimum-sum adjacent pair with its sum. Impose a cap K on how many times merge_min_pair() may be invoked. F2: set K to the true minimum number of merges t needed for the given nums; this is feasible by performing the deterministic sequence until the first non-decreasing state. F3: set K = t-1; infeasibility is certified because the operation and tie-break are deterministic, so after exactly t-1 merges there is a unique array state that (by definition of t) is still not non-decreasing, hence no strategy can succeed within the budget.

title: count-prefix-and-suffix-pairs-i
sketch: Restrict access so the algorithm can peek words[i] only for i < V; the suffix words[V..n-1] are never reachable. F2: Promise the hidden suffix consists only of distinct single-character strings whose characters are not equal to any complete word in the visible prefix; then no cross-boundary or within-suffix prefix-and-suffix pairs can exist, so the answer equals the count computed over the visible prefix alone. F3: With no guarantee about the hidden part, two completions sharing the same visible prefix can force different answers (e.g., visible prefix ["a"], hidden suffix [] gives 0, while hidden suffix ["a"] gives 1 via pair (0,1)), proving impossibility for any function of only the visible prefix.

title: count-symmetric-integers
sketch: Model [low..high] as a one-pass stream of integers x; the only memory is a fixed RegisterBank, and you must return the exact count of symmetric x. F2: give total register capacity just sufficient to encode the counter over 0..R (R=high−low+1), i.e., ceil(log2(R+1)) bits, plus a tiny constant scratch (a couple small registers) reused per x to compute the two half-digit sums. F3: reduce capacity so the counter has strictly fewer than ceil(log2(R+1)) bits; since there are R+1 possible outputs but fewer encodable states, by pigeonhole two different streams yield the same final register state yet require different counts, so exact counting is impossible under this memory cap.

title: find-the-number-of-good-pairs-i
sketch: Stream the input with a fixed RegisterBank and require a single pass: first stream nums2 and maintain a frequency table for values v in [1..50] (each counter in 0..m), then stream nums1 and, for each x divisible by k, add the sum of freq[d] over all divisors d of x/k; F2 makes this feasible by giving enough capacity for 50 counters (≈50*ceil(log2(m+1)) bits) plus an accumulator for the answer (ceil(log2(n*m+1)) bits). F3 shrinks the register capacity below what’s needed to encode all nums2 histograms (e.g., <50*ceil(log2(m+1)) bits), so two different nums2 distributions collide in state; pick k=1 and choose nums1 to consist only of a value v where the two histograms differ, yielding different true counts from the same internal state, proving impossibility by pigeonhole.

title: find-the-number-of-winning-players
sketch: Expose only the first L entries of pick; the rest of the stream is hidden/inaccessible. F2: Along with the visible prefix, provide per-player upper bounds rem[i] on how many additional picks they can have in the hidden suffix, and construct instances so that for every player not already a winner in the prefix, their current best color count plus rem[i] is still < i+1, making the final winner count equal to the prefix-determined winners. F3: Give no guarantees about the hidden suffix; pick a prefix where some player i has exactly i copies of a color, then construct two completions with the same visible prefix—one adds one more of that color in the hidden suffix (player i wins) and one adds none (player i does not)—yielding different true answers despite identical visibility, proving impossibility.

title: check-if-a-string-is-an-acronym-of-words
sketch: Restrict access so the agent can read all of s but only the first K words via peek_word(i) for i < K; any i >= K is inaccessible. F2: Set K = |s| and add a promise that words.length == K; then the answer is decidable from the visible part by checking words[i][0] == s[i] for all i and |s| == K. F3: Remove the promise; construct two full inputs sharing the same visible prefix (first K words whose initials equal s and K = |s|): (a) no extra hidden words (answer true), and (b) append one hidden extra word (answer false); since the visible views are identical, any function of the view cannot solve both, certifying impossibility.

title: make-a-square-with-the-same-color
sketch: Restrict to grid.peek(i,j) and a state-changing flip(i,j), with a cap on the number of flips. For F2, let D be the minimum over the four 2x2 sub-squares of min(#B, #W) within that square (in the original setting choose instances with D ≤ 1) and set the budget to D, which is sufficient by flipping the minority cells in the best 2x2. For F3, set the budget to D−1; infeasibility follows since each flip can fix at most one disagreeing cell in any chosen 2x2, so any 2x2 needs at least min(#B, #W) flips, and D is the minimum such requirement across all 2x2s.

title: apple-redistribution-into-boxes
sketch: Expose only a visible prefix of the capacity array via peek(i), i <= L, with the rest permanently hidden. F2: Promise that every hidden capacity is <= τ, where τ is the smallest capacity among the k largest capacities in the visible prefix that first make their sum >= total_apples; then the global minimal k equals that prefix-derived k (no unseen larger box can reduce k). F3: With no promise about the hidden suffix, two completions sharing the same visible prefix can require different answers (e.g., apple sum T=6, visible prefix capacities [3,3]; hidden A=[1,1] gives answer 2, hidden B=[6,1] gives answer 1), so no function of only the visible prefix can be correct on all inputs.

title: score-of-a-string
sketch: Stream the string with stream.next_char(), using only a fixed RegisterBank. F2: give exactly enough state to be feasible, e.g., two registers: R_prev in [0..25] to hold the previous letter’s index (5 bits) and R_sum in [0..25*(n-1)] to hold the running score (for n<=100, 0..2475, 12 bits), updating R_sum by adding |curr_idx - R_prev| each step. F3: reduce total capacity below this (e.g., make R_sum max 2047 or remove the ability to store all 26 prev values), so the bank has fewer states than the number of distinct (prev_char, partial_sum) pairs (or even than the 2476 possible final scores for n<=100); by pigeonhole, two inputs yield the same final register state but different true scores, so any decoder must output the same value for both, proving impossibility.

title: find-words-containing-character
sketch: Add a semantic constraint on the output: it must contain exactly K indices. F2: choose K to equal the true count of words containing x for the given input, so any valid solution naturally meets the size constraint. F3: choose K to be contradictory (e.g., true_count − 1); the certificate is the counted total c of matching indices—since any correct output must include exactly those c indices, no array of length K != c can be correct.

title: divisible-and-non-divisible-sums-difference
sketch: This is a straightforward arithmetic computation with a closed-form solution (sum 1..n minus twice the sum of multiples of m). There’s no natural unit operation whose budget tightly characterizes feasibility (C2), no inherent memory bottleneck since O(1) state suffices (C3), and no meaningful restricted-view variant with a certifiable impossibility without being artificial (C4). Any C1-style extra semantic rule (e.g., parity/prime constraints on the output) would be contrived rather than stemming from the task’s structure.

title: maximum-odd-binary-number
sketch: Stream the bits with stream.next_bit(), and allow only a fixed RegisterBank as memory; assume n = |s| is known. F2: give exactly B = ceil(log2(n+1)) bits of register capacity to count k = number of '1's, then output 1^(k-1) 0^(n-k) 1 — this is feasible with that capacity. F3: set B = ceil(log2(n+1)) - 1; by pigeonhole there exist two inputs of length n with different counts k and k' (both ≥1) mapping to the same register state, yet they require different outputs (different numbers of leading 1s), so no algorithm using only those registers can be correct on both — a certified infeasibility.

title: find-the-encrypted-string
sketch: Restrict the solver to an array interface with workspace.peek(i) and workspace.swap_adjacent(i) only, transforming the initial string (characters treated as distinct tokens by original index) into the k-rotation target t[i] = s[(i+k) mod n]. F2: impose a strict swap budget equal to the inversion count of the k’-rotation permutation (k’ = k mod n), which is k’*(n-k’); this is tight since each adjacent swap changes inversion count by at most 1. F3: set the budget to k’*(n-k’) - 1 for any case with 1 <= k’ <= n-1; infeasibility is certified by the inversion-count lower bound, as the required permutation has exactly k’*(n-k’) inversions.

title: find-x-sum-of-all-k-long-subarrays-i
sketch: Treat it as a single-pass stream.next() over nums with only a fixed RegisterBank for state. F2: allocate exactly enough registers to store a circular buffer of the last k values (each in [1..50]) plus one counter per value 1..50 (range [0..k]); on each next() update the outgoing/incoming counts via the buffer and compute the x-sum by scanning the 50 counters to select the top x under the (frequency, value) tie-break. F3: cap total register capacity below what’s needed to represent the window’s sufficient statistic (e.g., fewer than 50·ceil(log2(k+1)) bits for the frequency vector, or fewer than k·ceil(log2 50) bits for the ring buffer), forcing two distinct k-window multisets to collide in state; pick two such windows whose top-x sets (and thus x-sums) differ (e.g., one where a is most frequent vs another where b>a is), certifying impossibility by pigeonhole.

title: find-the-k-th-character-in-string-game-i
sketch: Restrict to an interface with workspace.expand() (state-changing: apply the next-letter transform to the whole current word and append) and workspace.peek(i) (read-only: returns the i-th character of the current word; errors if i > current length). F2: cap the number of expand() calls to ceil(log2 k), which is exactly the minimum needed since length starts at 1 and doubles each expand, making this bound tight. F3: cap expands at ceil(log2 k) - 1; after b expands the word has length 2^b < k, so peek(k) is unreachable and no sequence of allowed operations can produce the correct k-th character—certified infeasible by the length doubling invariant.

title: minimum-sum-of-mountain-triplets-i
sketch: Add an output-side rule: the returned minimum-sum mountain triplet must have its middle index j in a provided allowed set P (singleton P={j*} is fine). F2: choose P so that it contains the true optimal peak j_opt for the given input (and at least one valid peak), so the extra rule is satisfied without changing the answer. F3: choose P so that every j in P cannot be a peak on this input (e.g., pick j* with no i<j* s.t. nums[i]<nums[j*] or no k>j* s.t. nums[k]<nums[j*]); the certificate is the input itself plus a check over P showing the necessary left/right-smaller elements do not exist, hence no feasible triplet can satisfy the added rule.

title: transform-array-by-parity
sketch: Restrict the solver to first map nums to a binary array b (even→0, odd→1), then use only workspace.peek(i) and workspace.swap_adjacent(i) to sort b, counting each swap against a budget. F2: set the swap budget to the exact inversion count of b (number of 1-before-0 pairs), which is tight and sufficient. F3: set the budget to inversion_count(b)−1; this is unreachable because each adjacent swap can decrease the inversion count by at most 1, so any input with at least one inversion (e.g., [1,0] after mapping) certifies infeasibility.

title: count-the-number-of-incremovable-subarrays-i
sketch: F2: Restrict access to only a visible prefix (peek(i) allowed for i < P), but guarantee that the hidden suffix (i ≥ P) is strictly increasing, every hidden element is greater than every visible element, and n is known. Under this guarantee, the count is determined by the visible prefix and n alone: removals wholly in the suffix are all valid iff the visible prefix is strictly increasing; cross-boundary joins are always valid; and removals wholly in the prefix depend only on the visible prefix. F3: Remove any guarantees about the hidden part; then two arrays sharing the same visible prefix can require different answers, e.g., with visible prefix [2,1], nums=[2,1,3,4] has 7 incremovable subarrays while nums=[2,1,2,4] has 6, proving impossibility for any function of only the visible prefix.

title: maximum-containers-on-a-ship
sketch: Restrict the view so only n and w are visible while maxWeight is completely hidden. F2: add a promise that maxWeight >= n^2 * w (or, alternatively, maxWeight < w), which makes the answer determinable from the visible prefix alone (answer is n^2, or 0 respectively). F3: remove the promise; e.g., with visible (n=3, w=5) the hidden maxWeight could be 20 (answer 4) or 1000 (answer 9), two inputs sharing the same visible prefix but requiring different outputs, certifying impossibility.

title: find-the-original-typed-string-i
sketch: Restrict access so only a visible prefix of the word can be peeked; the rest of the string is hidden and unreachable. F2: Add a guarantee that the hidden suffix, if any, has no adjacent equal letters and its first hidden character differs from the last visible character; then every hidden character starts a new run, so 1 + |word| - runs = 1 + |prefix| - runs_in_prefix is computable from the prefix alone. F3: With no guarantee about the hidden part, two completions sharing the same visible prefix can force different true answers (e.g., prefix 'ab' could be completed as 'ab' with answer 1 or 'abb' with answer 2), so any function of only the visible prefix is provably impossible.

title: button-with-longest-push-time
sketch: Recast as a single-pass stream over (index, time), with the only memory a fixed RegisterBank. To be correct, the algorithm must retain the previous time, the best duration so far, the best index (for tie-breaking), and a 1-bit flag for whether the first event has been seen. F2: allocate exactly enough total bits to store these values (e.g., b=ceil(log2(max_time+1)) for times/durations and ceil(log2(max_index+1)) for indices; here b≈17, so prev_time b + best_duration b + best_index b + 1 flag), forcing tight packing but still feasible. F3: make total capacity insufficient to store prev_time exactly (or strictly less than the sum above), so two different previous times collide in state; then choose the next event with time t1=2t and indices a>b so that when prev_time=t the durations tie (pick b) but when prev_time=t+1 the first press wins (pick a), yielding two inputs with identical internal state just before the second event but requiring different outputs—impossible.

title: existence-of-a-substring-in-a-string-and-its-reverse
sketch: Restrict the view to only a prefix of s; the rest of the string is unreachable. F2: add a promise that the hidden suffix is a run of a single known character c of known length L, so the only unseen bigrams are the boundary (last_visible_char, c) and possibly (c,c) if L>=2—together with the visible prefix this fully determines whether any length-2 substring also appears in reverse(s). F3: without any promise, two strings with the same visible prefix can force different answers (e.g., with visible prefix "ab": s1="aba" yields true due to "ab"/"ba", while s2="abc" yields false), so no function of only the prefix can be correct on both.

title: remove-trailing-zeros-from-a-string
sketch: Restrict the interface to peek_last() and a single state-changing operation pop_last(), with a cap on how many pops are allowed. F2: set the pop budget exactly to T, the true number of trailing zeros in the given input; by peeking and popping only while the last char is '0', you use exactly T pops, which is provably tight since each pop removes at most one trailing zero. F3: set the pop budget to T-1 on a specific input (e.g., num='51230100' so T=2); with at most T-1 pops, at least one trailing zero necessarily remains, so any resulting string still ends with '0', proving infeasibility.

title: harshad-number
sketch: Restrict access to the decimal representation so that peek(i) is only allowed for i ≤ L (a visible prefix); digits beyond L are unreachable. F2: add a guarantee that the hidden suffix is all zeros and its length m is known, so both the digit sum s = sum(prefix) and x = prefix*10^m are computable from the visible part, letting us decide Harshad and output s or -1. F3: with no guarantees, two numbers can share the same visible prefix but require different outputs (e.g., with L=1, 18 and 19 both show prefix "1" yet the true answers are 9 and -1 respectively), proving impossibility for any function of only the visible prefix.

title: ant-on-the-boundary
sketch: Stream nums with only a fixed-size RegisterBank; to be correct you must maintain the running position s in [-10n,10n] and the return count c in [0,n]. F2: allocate B = ceil(log2((20n+1)*(n+1))) bits (enough to uniquely encode every (s,c) pair) and pack/unpack s and c each step to update and test s==0, incrementing c accordingly. F3: give B one bit less; by pigeonhole two different prefixes with distinct (s,c) share the same register state, and fixing the very next element v = -s (with identical suffix thereafter) makes one continuation hit the boundary (incrementing c) while the other does not, so the algorithm—starting from the same internal state and seeing the same suffix—must output the same count on both, a contradiction.

title: maximum-strong-pair-xor-i
sketch: Use a prefix-restricted view: the solver can peek(i) only within a visible prefix; the suffix is never accessible. F2: add a promise about the hidden suffix that makes the answer depend only on the visible part, e.g., every hidden element is > 2*max(visible) and the hidden suffix itself is strictly increasing with each next > 2*previous; then no strong pair can involve any hidden element except (h,h) which yields XOR 0, so the maximum XOR is determined entirely by pairs within the visible prefix. F3: with no promise, two arrays sharing the same visible prefix can require different answers, e.g., prefix [1] with hidden A = [1] gives max XOR 0 (only (1,1)), while prefix [1] with hidden B = [2,3] gives max XOR 3 (pair (1,2)), proving impossibility for any function of only the visible prefix.

title: minimum-operations-to-collect-elements
sketch: Expose only peek(i) (free) and pop_last() (counted) and require the agent to actually collect values {1..k} by popping from the end. F2: set the pop budget B to the true minimum m* = n − min_{v in [1..k]} rightmost_index(v), forcing an optimal strategy that pops exactly until the earliest among the rightmost occurrences of 1..k is exposed. F3: set B = m* − 1; infeasible because there exists v* with last occurrence at index p = argmin rightmost_index, and with fewer than n − p pops v* cannot be collected—(v*, p) serves as the certificate.

title: make-three-strings-equal
sketch: Use an interface with read-only peeks (e.g., length and char-at) and a single state-changing operation delete_rightmost(s_i), and impose a hard cap on how many deletions may be performed. F2: set the deletion budget B to the exact minimum needed, B = |s1|+|s2|+|s3| - 3·L where L is the length (≥1) of the common longest prefix of s1, s2, and s3; this is feasible and tight. F3: set B = (|s1|+|s2|+|s3| - 3·L) - 1 on an instance with L≥1; this is impossible since each operation reduces the total length sum by exactly 1, but any valid equalization to a common prefix requires at least |s1|+|s2|+|s3| - 3·L deletions.

title: maximum-unique-subarray-sum-after-deletion
sketch: Model it as a single-pass stream with only a fixed RegisterBank for memory; the goal reduces to summing each distinct positive value once (if any), else 0 if a zero appears, else the maximum (least negative) value. F2: Promise that the input has at most K distinct positive values and give a RegisterBank with K slots that can store values in [-100,100] plus O(1) registers for the running sum, a zero-seen flag, and the current max negative; on each x>0, add x the first time it’s seen by scanning the K slots and storing it, else skip; track zero and max negative, then output sum/0/maxneg accordingly. F3: Remove that promise and cap the RegisterBank so its total number of representable states is < 5151; since the correct output over all inputs can be any integer in [-100,5050] (5151 possibilities), by pigeonhole two inputs with different true answers map to the same final state, so exact computation is impossible.

title: longest-strictly-increasing-or-strictly-decreasing-subarray
sketch: Restrict access so the agent can peek only the first k elements of nums; indices > k are unreachable. F2: provide the guarantee that the true longest strictly increasing/decreasing subarray lies entirely within the first k elements (equivalently, e.g., the hidden suffix is constant equal to nums[k]), so the answer is determined by the visible prefix. F3: no guarantee; pick a fixed visible prefix P (e.g., [1,2]) and two completions with identical prefix but different suffixes, such as A = [1,2,3,4,5] (answer 5) and B = [1,2,2,2,2] (answer 2), proving impossibility for any function of only the visible part.

title: find-common-elements-between-two-arrays
sketch: Restrict access so the solver may peek only a visible prefix of each array (k1 of nums1 and k2 of nums2). F2: set k1 = n (nums1 fully visible) and k2 < m with the guarantee that every hidden nums2 element is a value not present in nums1; then A equals the number of nums1 indices whose values lie in the visible nums2 prefix, and B equals the number of visible nums2 indices whose values lie in nums1—both determined from the visible data. F3: keep k1 = n and k2 < m but remove the guarantee; two completions sharing the same visible prefixes—(i) hidden nums2 suffix disjoint from nums1 and (ii) hidden suffix containing some v ∈ nums1 absent from the visible prefix—yield different A (increases by count_nums1(v)) and B (increases by the number of hidden v’s), so no function of the visible part can be correct.

title: reverse-degree-of-a-string
sketch: Restrict access so peek(i) is only allowed for i ≤ K (the rest of the string is unreachable) and the total length n is known. F2: additionally guarantee that every hidden suffix character (i > K) is a fixed known letter, e.g., all 'z', so the suffix’s weighted contribution Σ_{i=K+1..n} i*rev('z') is known and the overall reverse degree is computable from the visible prefix plus this constant. F3: with no guarantee on the hidden suffix, two strings sharing the same visible prefix p (e.g., p + 'a'⋯ vs p + 'z'⋯) yield different sums, so any algorithm depending only on the visible part cannot be correct on both, certifying impossibility.

title: sum-of-good-numbers
sketch: Stream the array once with a fixed-size RegisterBank; maintain a ring buffer of exactly k pending items, each storing (nums[i] in [1..1000], and a 1-bit flag left_ok = [nums[i] > nums[i-k] or i<k]). On reading index t, finalize item t-k by checking stored value against nums[t] and adding to the sum if both conditions hold, then enqueue (nums[t], left_ok); after the stream, flush the remaining k items whose right check is vacuously true. F3: If the bank has fewer than k value slots (or fewer total bits than needed to distinguish all k-tuples of values plus k flags), two different prefixes with distinct last-k windows collapse to the same state; choose a common suffix that makes exactly one of the differing indices good by setting its right neighbor above/below, yielding different correct sums while the machine’s state (hence output) must be identical—an information-theoretic impossibility.

title: minimum-element-after-replacement-with-digit-sum
sketch: Make it a single-pass stream over nums (stream.next_int()), with the only persistent memory a RegisterBank. F2: allocate exactly enough capacity to represent any possible digit-sum minimum (1..36) and a running accumulator, e.g., two 6-bit registers; compute each digit sum ephemerally, update the 6-bit running min, and return it. F3: reduce capacity below what can encode all possible minima (e.g., only 5 bits for the min); by pigeonhole, there are 36 possible outputs but ≤32 encodable states, so two inputs with different true minima must end in the same register state, forcing any algorithm to output the same value on both—certifying infeasibility.

title: count-partitions-with-even-sum-difference
sketch: Restrict access so the solver can only peek the first k elements (known n, suffix i>k is unreachable). F2: additionally provide the parity of the hidden suffix’s sum (equivalently, the total-sum parity); since the answer is n-1 if total is even and 0 otherwise, this guarantee makes the result decidable from the visible prefix. F3: with no guarantee, pick two arrays sharing the same visible prefix and n but whose hidden suffix sums have opposite parity; they require different outputs (n-1 vs 0), so any function of only the visible prefix is provably impossible.

title: number-of-changing-keys
sketch: Use a single-pass stream API (stream.next_char()) with a fixed RegisterBank; in F2, allow exactly enough bits to hold the last key lowercased (5 bits for 26 letters) and a counter up to |s| (ceil(log2(|s|+1)) bits), using only registers.get/set. In F3, reduce the total capacity below 5 + ceil(log2(|s|+1)) bits so the bank can represent fewer than 26*(|s|+1) distinct (last_key, count_so_far) states; by pigeonhole two different prefixes collide, and by choosing the next character (matching one last_key or differing) and then terminating, the true final counts differ, proving impossibility. F1 uses the same interface with generous capacity (e.g., a 5-bit last-key register plus an 8-bit counter).

title: minimum-average-of-smallest-and-largest-elements
sketch: Expose only workspace.peek_min(), workspace.peek_max() (non-mutating) and a single mutating op pop_pair() that removes the current global min and max and returns their average; the task is to return the minimum of all returned averages. F2: impose an operation budget of exactly n/2 calls to pop_pair() (tight: you can compute every average and track the min within this budget). F3: budget n/2 - 1, which is impossible because each pop_pair reveals at most one average and you cannot see beyond the current extremes without popping; construct two inputs that produce the same first n/2 - 1 extreme pairs but have different last pair averages (e.g., keep a1,a2,a_{n-1},a_n identical while varying only a_{n/2},a_{n/2+1}), so any algorithm with ≤ n/2 - 1 pops has identical observations yet the true answer differs, certifying infeasibility.

title: find-the-losers-of-the-circular-game
sketch: Add an extra semantic requirement: the output losers list must include a required set R of friend indices. F2: pick R to be any subset of the true losers for the given (n, k), so the standard correct losers list already satisfies the added inclusion constraint. F3: include at least one friend guaranteed to have received the ball (e.g., friend 1) in R; since friend 1 always receives the ball at the start, requiring 1 to be a loser is impossible, providing a direct contradiction certificate.

title: snake-in-matrix
sketch: Stream the commands with a single-pass interface (stream.next_cmd()), and restrict memory to a fixed-size RegisterBank. F2: give exactly B = ceil(log2(n^2)) bits of total register capacity (e.g., one B-bit register) so the solver can store the flat index p in [0, n^2-1] and update p with +1/-1/±n per command, then output p. F3: reduce capacity to B-1 bits; by pigeonhole there are fewer than n^2 distinct register states but n^2 distinct reachable final cells (e.g., [] -> 0 and ["RIGHT"] -> 1 for n>=2), so two different command sequences must end with the same register state yet require different outputs, making correctness impossible.

title: account-balance-after-rounded-purchase
sketch: Restrict information by exposing only the visible prefix of the decimal string for purchaseAmount (all digits except the final units digit); the hidden suffix is the last digit and is never accessible. F2: keep this view but promise the hidden units digit is in {0,1,2,3,4}, so rounding always goes down to 10*visible_prefix and the balance 100 - 10*visible_prefix is uniquely determined. F3: same restricted view with no promise; e.g., purchaseAmount=14 and 16 share the same visible prefix "1" but require different balances (90 vs 80), so no function of only the visible prefix can be correct.

title: most-frequent-ids
sketch: This is a dynamic frequency-tracking/data-structure problem; none of C1–C4 map cleanly without contrived interfaces or guarantees. C1 would require adding artificial semantic constraints (e.g., monotonicity) that contradict valid instances; C2 lacks a natural primitive-and-tight budget like adjacent swaps; C3’s clean pigeonhole-style memory threshold isn’t natural because many internal states share the same max, and C4’s prefix-view either trivializes (answers depend only on the seen prefix) or becomes artificial by hiding parts of the needed prefix.

title: maximum-possible-number-by-binary-concatenation
sketch: Augment the task with pairwise precedence constraints over indices (i,j): the final concatenation must place nums[i]’s binary block before nums[j]’s block, in addition to still achieving the globally maximum concatenation value. F2: choose only pairs consistent with at least one globally maximizing order (e.g., those implied by sorting the three binaries by the comparator xy > yx on concatenation), so the same maximum remains attainable while respecting all pairs. F3: inject a single contradictory pair (pick i,j with bin(nums[i])+bin(nums[j]) > bin(nums[j])+bin(nums[i]) but require j before i); certificate: compute these two-length concatenations to show a strict inequality, implying any full permutation with j before i yields a strictly smaller concatenation than one with i before j, so no output can both be the global maximum and satisfy the pair.

title: find-the-count-of-numbers-which-are-not-special
sketch: This is a purely number-theoretic counting task (numbers with exactly two proper divisors are precisely prime squares), relying on arithmetic properties of [l, r]. It doesn’t naturally involve an operation budget, fixed workspace over a stream, or a restricted-view input; adding any of C1–C4 would require artificial constraints (e.g., oracle query budgets or hiding r), not inherent to the problem’s structure.

title: maximize-the-profit-as-the-salesman
sketch: Add a semantic constraint that certain offers must be included in the chosen set. F2: designate a set M of required offers that are pairwise non-overlapping on this instance; the task is to maximize gold subject to including all of M, which is feasible because M is consistent with the base disjointness rule. F3: designate a required set M′ that contains at least one pair of overlapping offers (their intervals intersect); this is provably impossible since different buyers can’t buy the same house—certificate is the indices and ranges of the conflicting pair, whose overlap contradicts feasibility for any valid solution.

title: longest-non-decreasing-subarray-from-two-arrays
sketch: Model it as a single-pass stream over pairs (nums1[i], nums2[i]) with a fixed RegisterBank; the optimal DP needs to keep only: the two previous element values (the last nums1[i−1], nums2[i−1]) and the two DP lengths ending at i−1 (len1, len2), plus the running best. F2: give exactly enough capacity to store these 5 integers (e.g., two registers of ⌈log2(maxA)⌉ bits for the values and three of ⌈log2(n+1)⌉ bits for lengths), which suffices for the standard O(1)-memory DP update. F3: remove even a single bit from the capacity needed to distinguish the previous values (or force prev1/prev2 to share a register), so there exist two prefixes with identical register state but different true prev values a<b; on the next pair choose x with a≤x<b so one instance can extend while the other cannot, yielding different correct DP transitions—by pigeonhole, any algorithm must err on one of them.

title: minimum-number-of-operations-to-make-array-empty
sketch: Model the input as a single-pass stream.next(), and the algorithm may only use a fixed RegisterBank of R registers (each b-bit integer) to maintain state. F2: set R and b just large enough to store exact per-value frequency counts for this instance (e.g., allocate two registers per distinct value: one for the key and one for its count; require R >= 2D and b >= max{ceil(log2(max(nums)+1)), ceil(log2(n+1))}), which lets you compute the exact sum over values of the minimal 2/3-deletion ops (or detect a singleton => -1). F3: reduce capacity so R < 2D or b is too small to hold some needed key/count; by pigeonhole, two inputs that differ only in turning some value’s count from 1 to 2 (changing the answer from -1 to feasible) must collide into the same register state, so no RegisterBank-limited algorithm can always output the correct minimum — certified infeasible by a state-count argument.

title: find-the-n-th-value-after-k-seconds
sketch: This task reduces to computing a binomial coefficient C(n+k-1, n-1) modulo 1e9+7 (or via a straightforward DP), with input consisting of just two integers. There is no natural operation-budget analogue with a tight, provable lower bound like inversion count (C2) without inventing an artificial API; no meaningful streaming/state-memory bound (C3) since the input is not a stream and O(1)/O(n) solutions exist; and no natural restricted-view (C4) because hiding part of {n,k} just makes the function indeterminate in a trivial way. C1 would also be artificial, requiring extra semantic rules unrelated to the problem’s inherent structure.

title: find-the-length-of-the-longest-common-prefix
sketch: Restrict access so the solver can only peek the first K1 elements of arr1 and first K2 elements of arr2; the remaining suffixes are never accessible. F2: add a promise that every hidden element’s set of digit-prefixes is a subset of the prefixes already seen in the visible portion of the same array, so any longest common prefix achievable with hidden items is already realizable with visible items, making the answer determined by what’s visible. F3: with no such guarantee, two completions sharing the identical visible prefix can require different answers (e.g., visible arr1=[12], arr2=[34]; completion A adds 1200 to arr2 giving answer 2, while completion B adds only numbers starting with 5 to arr2 giving answer 0), proving impossibility for any function of only the visible part.

title: find-the-maximum-length-of-a-good-subsequence-i
sketch: Tighten the output’s semantic validity by requiring that the returned good subsequence must include a designated set S of indices from nums (respecting original order). F2: pick S whose induced sequence in nums has at most k unequal-adjacent pairs (e.g., lies within ≤ k+1 runs), ensuring feasibility and allowing the solver to extend around S to maximize length. F3: inject one extra required index so that the values on S force k+1 unequal-adjacent pairs; any subsequence including S must then have ≥ k+1 transitions, certifying impossibility under the ≤ k constraint by simply exhibiting S and counting its forced transitions.

title: minimum-number-of-operations-to-make-word-k-periodic
sketch: Expose only block_peek(b) to read the length-k block at block index b and copy_block(dst,src) as the single state-changing operation, with a hard cap on how many copies may be performed. F2: set the budget B = m − f_max, where m = n/k and f_max is the maximum frequency of any existing length-k block; it is always achievable by copying the majority block into each of the other blocks. F3: set the budget to B−1; the certificate is an input with maximum block frequency f_max < m, and the invariant that each copy can increase the count of the chosen target block by at most 1, so reaching m identical blocks requires at least m − f_max copies, making B−1 provably insufficient.

title: minimum-array-changes-to-make-differences-equal
sketch: Use a restricted interface: peek(i) to read and set(i, v) to replace an element with v in [0..k]; count only set() as the state-changing operation under a budget. F2: set the operation budget to M, the true minimum number of element changes needed to achieve a uniform X across symmetric pairs for this instance—feasible and tight. F3: set the budget to M-1; certificate: let A* be an optimal target array with |A*[i]-A*[n-1-i]|=X*, the Hamming distance from the input to A* is M, and each set() changes at most one position, so no sequence of ≤ M-1 writes can reach any valid target.

title: make-string-a-subsequence-using-cyclic-increments
sketch: Restrict the interface to read-only peeks of str1/str2 and a single state-changing operation mark_for_increment(i) (at most once per index), with a global apply that increments all marked positions by +1 mod 26; the algorithm must decide if str2 is a subsequence of the transformed str1 under a cap of K marks. F2: set K to the true minimum number of indices in str1 that must be incremented to realize some subsequence alignment with str2 (tight budget). F3: set K to that minimum minus one; impossibility certificate is that each mark can fix at most one required +1 mismatch in any valid alignment, so with fewer than the minimum marks no alignment can satisfy all needed character matches.

title: ways-to-split-array-into-good-subarrays
sketch: Augment the counting task with semantic constraints on which split boundaries are allowed: require that certain indices must be cut positions in the partition into good subarrays. F2: provide a set S of required cut indices such that S contains at most one index inside each zero-run between consecutive 1s (and none before the first 1 or after the last 1); this is consistent with the base rule, fixing those gaps while leaving others free, so the count becomes the product over the unspecified gaps of (gap+1). F3: inject a required cut outside any between-ones zero-run (e.g., in the all-zero prefix/suffix) or require two distinct cuts within the same zero-run; certificate: in any valid partition there is exactly one cut per zero-run between consecutive 1s and none elsewhere, so the imposed cut(s) would force a subarray with 0 or 2 ones, making the specification impossible.

title: neighboring-bitwise-xor
sketch: Stream the derived bits via stream.next_bit() and allow only a fixed-size RegisterBank as memory. F2: give a memory budget of exactly 1 bit total; maintain a running XOR of the stream and at end return true iff the accumulator is 0 (this is tight for this problem). F3: give a memory budget with capacity < 1 bit (only one state); then no single-pass algorithm can compute parity—e.g., derived=[1,0] (parity 1⇒false) and derived=[0,0] (parity 0⇒true) share the same last symbol, but with 0 bits of memory the final state/output cannot distinguish them, yielding a contradiction (pigeonhole/information-theoretic certificate).

title: sum-in-a-matrix
sketch: Restrict the solver to a row-heap interface: for each row only row.peek_max() (free) and row.pop_max() (the single state-changing op) are available; the underlying arrays are otherwise inaccessible. F2: set the pop_max budget to T = sum_i len(row_i); simulate the process exactly (pop once per non-empty row per round), which is feasible and tight since revealing the k-th item of any row requires k pops in that row. F3: budget T-1; construct two inputs identical on all elements except one row’s final (last-round) element is 0 vs 1 while all other rows’ final elements are 0—after T-1 pops that last element remains hidden but it changes the last-round maximum, so no algorithm using this interface can always return the correct final score.

title: length-of-the-longest-subsequence-that-sums-to-target
sketch: F2: Present nums as a single-pass stream.next_int(), and allow only a fixed RegisterBank with get/set on fixed-width registers; total capacity is exactly (target+1)*ceil(log2(n+2)) bits to store dp[0..target] as the best achievable lengths in {-1,0..n}, enabling a tight in-place 0/1 knapsack update (reverse s) and correct output at end. F3: Reduce capacity to fewer than (target+1)*ceil(log2(n+2)) bits (e.g., minus 1 bit); by pigeonhole, some two distinct DP states after a prefix collide in the registers—choose an s where their best lengths differ and append a suffix containing exactly target−s (plus numbers >target as dummies) so the final optimal lengths must differ, yielding a certified impossibility under that memory budget.

title: maximum-energy-boost-from-two-drinks
sketch: Restrict access so the solver can only peek the first p entries of each array; indices i >= p are unreachable. F2: add a promise that for all i >= p, energyDrinkA[i] = energyDrinkB[i] = 0, so the optimal total is determined entirely by the visible prefix (compute the DP on the prefix; the hidden part contributes nothing and there’s no boundary ambiguity). F3: remove the promise; exhibit two completions sharing the same visible prefix but with different true answers, e.g., n=3, p=2 with prefix A[0..1]=[4,1], B[0..1]=[1,1]. Completion 1: A[2]=1, B[2]=3 yields optimum 7 (A, wait, B). Completion 2: A[2]=100, B[2]=1 yields optimum 105 (always A). Any function of only the visible prefix must give one number, so it cannot be correct for both, proving impossibility.

title: continuous-subarrays
sketch: Expose only a fixed visible prefix via peek(i) for i < P; the suffix i >= P is never observable. F2: Promise that all hidden suffix values lie in an interval disjoint by ≥3 from all visible-prefix values (e.g., min(suffix) ≥ max(prefix)+3 or max(suffix) ≤ min(prefix)−3), and also that the suffix’s global range ≤2. Then no cross-boundary subarray can be continuous, and the suffix contributes exactly L*(L+1)/2 with L=n−P, so the total is determinable from the prefix and L. F3: Remove the promise; two arrays with the same visible prefix can yield different totals (e.g., same prefix A, suffix S1 far from A so no crossing windows, vs suffix S2 equal to last prefix value so all cross-boundary subarrays are continuous), proving impossibility from the prefix alone.

title: hash-divided-string
sketch: Stream s via stream.next_char() with only a fixed RegisterBank as memory. F2: provide just enough capacity to hold (a) the running sum mod 26 for the current block (5 bits) and (b) a counter for position within the block 0..k-1 (ceil(log2 k) bits); this suffices to emit one hashed char every k reads and reset. F3: reduce total capacity below 5 + ceil(log2 k) bits (e.g., only 4 bits for the remainder), forcing two distinct remainders to share a state; then pick two k-length substrings with sums differing by 1 (e.g., start with 'a' vs 'b' and fill the rest with 'a's) which must produce different outputs, but the algorithm cannot distinguish them from the same state, proving impossibility by pigeonhole/indistinguishability.

title: shortest-and-lexicographically-smallest-beautiful-string
sketch: Stream s left-to-right using only a fixed RegisterBank; the output must be the shortest substring with exactly k ones, breaking ties lexicographically. F2: give the bank capacity of at least len bits (plus O(log n) counters), where len is the shortest-beautiful length for this input; keep a sliding k-ones window and, whenever a candidate beats the current best in length or tie-breaks lexicographically, overwrite the bank with that window’s bits—at end, emit the bank contents. F3: cap the bank to fewer than len bits; then there exist two inputs that are identical up to the final window but whose unique shortest-beautiful substrings (of length len) differ, forcing any single-pass algorithm with < len bits to collide on internal states yet require different L-bit outputs—by pigeonhole, it’s impossible to always output the correct substring.

title: find-the-lexicographically-smallest-valid-sequence
sketch: Restrict access so the algorithm can only peek the first L characters of word1; the rest of word1 is hidden/unreachable while it must still output the lexicographically smallest valid index sequence for the full strings. F2: add a promise that the hidden suffix contains at least |word2| occurrences of every lowercase letter (i.e., an ample supply), so any earliest feasible choices made within the visible prefix can always be completed, making the answer determinable from the prefix alone. F3: with no promise, two inputs sharing the same visible prefix can force different answers (e.g., word2="ab", visible prefix P="c"; one suffix S_good contains a 'b' so picking index 0 and using the single mismatch on 'a' is feasible, while another suffix S_bad has no 'b', forcing the first index to shift to a later 'a'), proving impossibility for any function of only the visible part.

title: find-a-safe-walk-through-a-grid
sketch: Restrict access to the grid to a row-major visible prefix: peek(k) is allowed only for k < P; all cells with index ≥ P are unpeekable (hidden). F2: add a global promise that every hidden cell is 0 (safe), so the decision reduces to whether there exists a path from (0,0) to any boundary cell of the visible region using ≤ health−1 ones within the visible part (after crossing into the hidden all-zero suffix, reaching (m−1,n−1) is always possible at zero further cost). F3: remove any hidden-part guarantee; construct two instances identical on the first P cells where in one the hidden suffix contains a zero corridor to the target within budget, and in the other the hidden suffix blocks all such routes or forces > health−1 ones—since both share the same visible prefix, any function of only the visible part must output the same value on both, yielding a certificate of impossibility.

title: maximum-number-that-sum-of-the-prices-is-less-than-or-equal-to-k
sketch: Expose only a streaming interface over numbers 1,2,3,…: peek() reveals the price of the next number (count of set bits at positions multiple of x), and the single state-changing op advance() consumes that number, irrevocably adding its price to the running total; the answer num must equal how many advances were performed. F2: cap the number of advance() calls to the true optimum OPT (the greatest num with cumulative price ≤ k); greedily advance while the sum permits—this is feasible and tight because each advance increases num by at most 1. F3: cap advance() at OPT−1; it is impossible to return the true greatest num since reaching num=OPT requires at least OPT advances (each advance increases num by ≤1), so any strategy yields num≤OPT−1, a direct contradiction.

title: count-days-without-meetings
sketch: Restrict access so the solver can peek meetings[i] only for i ≤ k; the remaining intervals are never reachable. F2: promise that every hidden interval (i > k) is fully contained in the union of the first k intervals, so the uncovered-day count is determined by days minus the covered length of the visible prefix’s union. F3: drop that promise; e.g., with days=10 and visible prefix [[2,4]], suffix A=[] yields answer 7 while suffix B=[[1,10]] yields answer 0, so two full inputs share the same visible part but need different outputs—proving impossibility under the restricted view.

title: count-submatrices-with-equal-frequency-of-x-and-y
sketch: Restrict access to only a top-left R×C prefix via peek(i,j); for F2, guarantee that every cell outside that prefix is '.', so any (0,0)-anchored submatrix’s X/Y counts are fully determined by the visible prefix and the known grid dimensions, making the total computable without reading hidden cells. For F3, with no guarantee about the hidden area, take the same visible 1×1 prefix with grid[0][0]='X': completion A fills all hidden cells with '.', yielding 0 valid submatrices, while completion B sets (0,1)='Y' and others '.', yielding at least one valid submatrix ((0,0)-(0,1)), proving impossibility from the prefix alone.

title: apply-operations-to-make-string-empty
sketch: Treat s as a single-pass stream and allow only a fixed RegisterBank. F2: allocate just enough capacity to store, for each of the 26 letters, its running count and current last-seen index (26 counts + 26 indices, each needing ⌈log2(n+1)⌉ bits), then after the pass compute R = max count and output the letters whose count=R sorted by their stored last indices. F3: make the total register capacity smaller than what’s needed to even distinguish all possible outputs (e.g., fewer than log2(26!) bits, since when all 26 letters tie, the final string can be any permutation of 26), so by pigeonhole there exist two inputs with different correct answers inducing the same register state, proving impossibility.

title: find-the-minimum-amount-of-time-to-brew-potions
sketch: This is a no‑wait flow‑shop makespan computation with p_ij = skill[i]*mana[j]; the minimal time depends on global interactions across all consecutive mana pairs and the full set of skill prefix sums. There’s no natural single primitive operation with a tight monotone budget (C2), no clean fixed small‑state streaming formulation without storing Θ(n) structure or rescanning (C3), and no partial‑view prefix that determines the answer absent strong, artificial promises (C4). Adding extra semantic output requirements (C1) would be contrived (e.g., parity or schedule shape constraints), not inherent to the task.

title: collecting-chocolates
sketch: Expose only peek_cost(i), buy(i), and a single capped state-changing op rotate_all() (cost x) that advances all types by +1 mod n. F2: cap the number of rotates at B = r*, the smallest r in [0..n−1] minimizing f(r) = r*x + sum_i min_{t∈[0..r]} nums[(i−t) mod n]; the global optimum is attainable within this budget and any schedule with fewer rotates cannot match it. F3: choose an instance whose first (strict) minimizer r* > 0 and set B = r*−1; then the best achievable with the cap is min_{r≤B} f(r) > f(r*), certifying impossibility of attaining the true optimum under the operation budget.

title: mark-elements-on-array-by-performing-queries
sketch: Model the queries as a single-pass stream and allow only a fixed RegisterBank as working memory. F2: allow exactly n bits to track which indices are marked (plus O(log sum) for the running sum); implement by repeatedly rescanning nums to pick the k_i smallest unmarked elements (tie-broken by index), flipping their bits and updating the sum—no heap or extra arrays. F3: reduce capacity to n-1 bits for the mark set; by pigeonhole, two different marked-subsets after some prefix collide in state—pick the next query as [j,0] where j differs between those subsets; with positive nums (e.g., distinct), the correct next answer differs by nums[j], so any algorithm with < n bits cannot be correct on all inputs.

title: maximum-palindromes-after-operations
sketch: The task is an allocation/optimization over the global multiset of characters and word-length parities. C2 is unnatural because there’s no canonical, provably tight minimal number of swaps to reach the optimum (the minimal swap count depends on an arbitrary target redistribution and isn’t a simple monotone resource like inversions). C1 would require adding extra per-position/output constraints that are artificial to the objective; C3 doesn’t match since the algorithm just needs small, fixed counting state (no pigeonhole tension); C4’s visibility restrictions would make the answer non-determinable from any natural prefix, so F1/F2 would hinge on contrived guarantees about hidden content.

title: find-the-sequence-of-strings-appeared-on-the-screen
sketch: Restrict the agent to only two operations on a screen state: press1() appends 'a' and press2() increments the last character cyclically, and require emitting the screen after each press. F2: impose an operation budget B = |target| + sum_i (ord(target[i]) - ord('a')) and require finishing in exactly B presses; this equals the minimal presses needed for any target under these operations. F3: set the budget to B-1; this is impossible because each press reduces the remaining deficit Φ(s) (the minimal presses still needed from s to target) by at most 1 and Φ("") = B, so after B-1 presses Φ > 0 (equivalently, you need at least |target| appends plus at least ord(target[i]) - ord('a') increments for each position i).

title: apply-operations-to-make-two-strings-equal
sketch: Restrict the interface to peeks into s1/s2 and a single state-changing operation flip_pair(i,j) that flips s1[i] and s1[j]; disallow the adjacent flip. Work only by calling flip_pair, under a cap on how many times it may be invoked, to achieve s1 == s2. F2: For instances with m = HammingDistance(s1,s2) even, set the budget to m/2; this is feasible by arbitrarily pairing the m mismatch positions, and tight because each flip_pair can reduce the mismatch count by at most 2. F3: On those same instances, set the budget to m/2 - 1; this is impossible with a certificate from the potential function (number of mismatches), which starts at m and decreases by at most 2 per operation, so reaching 0 requires at least m/2 calls.

title: find-mirror-score-of-a-string
sketch: Stream s left-to-right and allow only a fixed RegisterBank to store indices of currently-unmatched occurrences; correctness requires a LIFO stack of indices per letter so that when seeing c you can pop the most-recent unmatched mirror(c) and add i−j. F2: provision exactly 26·B registers of ⌈log2 n⌉ bits (or equivalent capacity) and promise that at any time the unmatched backlog per mirror pair never exceeds B, so these stacks fit and the greedy score is computable. F3: cap capacity below what’s needed for B+1 backlogged indices for some pair (e.g., (a,z)); then an input with B+1 a’s at positions p1<…<p_{B+1} followed by B+1 z’s forces storing all p’s, and with fewer than (B+1)·⌈log2 n⌉ bits two different {p_t} sets collide in register state but yield different total scores (sum of q_t−p_{B+2−t}), proving impossibility by pigeonhole.

title: sort-matrix-by-diagonals
sketch: Augment the task with extra relative-order constraints on element positions within the same diagonal: for selected pairs of original cells (r1,c1),(r2,c2) that lie on one diagonal, require that after sorting that diagonal (read in a fixed direction, e.g., top-left to bottom-right), the element from (r1,c1) appears before the one from (r2,c2). F2: choose only pairs whose values are already consistent with the required diagonal order (on bottom-left diagonals require v(r1,c1) >= v(r2,c2); on top-right require v(r1,c1) <= v(r2,c2)), so both the diagonal-sorting rule and the pairwise constraints can be satisfied. F3: inject at least one pair that contradicts the required order (e.g., on a bottom-left diagonal where v(a)<v(b), require a before b), and certify infeasibility by pointing to that diagonal and those two cells: any valid diagonal sort forces the opposite relative order, so no output can satisfy both.

title: find-longest-special-substring-that-occurs-thrice-i
sketch: Model a single-pass stream.next_char() with a fixed RegisterBank of bounded-range integers. F2: give just enough registers to maintain, for each of the 26 letters, its top-3 run lengths (plus O(1) for the current run), which suffices because the maximum k is the largest integer with sum_i max(0, r_i−k+1)≥3 and this depends only on the top three runs per letter. F3: reduce capacity so you cannot encode three run lengths per letter (e.g., only enough for top-2 or by shrinking integer ranges); by pigeonhole, two strings that agree on all stored state but differ in the third-largest run for some letter (chosen to flip whether k>r3 is achievable via extra windows from the largest run) will require different outputs, so no algorithm using this memory can always be correct.

title: largest-element-in-an-array-after-merge-operations
sketch: Model this as a single-pass left-to-right stream with only a fixed RegisterBank as memory. The canonical optimal solution maintains a monotone stack of segment sums (push current, then while top<=cur merge), so the required workspace equals the maximum stack height encountered on the given input. F2: set the number of registers exactly to that maximum height; the solver can implement the stack within the registers to compute the optimal largest final element. F3: reduce registers by one and use an input that forces that peak height and where later small items trigger long merge cascades; with only k-1 registers two distinct stack states after some prefix must collide (pigeonhole), and appending tailored suffixes yields different final answers, proving impossibility under the restricted memory.

title: count-special-subsequences
sketch: The output is a single global count of 4-index patterns, so there’s no natural C1-style semantic add-on (like extra ordering constraints) to the output itself. There’s also no obvious C2-style primitive operation with a tight per-operation progress bound analogous to swaps/inversions. A C3 single-pass RegisterBank threshold is not clean here because exact counting typically needs two-sided/global correlations; any lower bound would be contrived and input-distribution–dependent. Finally, C4 prefix-only access can easily produce F3 counterexamples, but any F1/F2 guarantee that makes the count determinable from the visible prefix would be trivial/unnatural (e.g., effectively revealing the whole array).

title: maximum-xor-product
sketch: Restrict access so the solver can only peek the top m of the n controllable bits of a and b (bits n-1 down to n-m); the remaining n-m lower bits are completely hidden/inaccessible. F2: add a promise that every hidden bit position i has a_i = b_i = 0, so the optimal choice on those positions is deterministically x_i = 1 and their contribution is fixed; thus the maximum is computable from the visible prefix alone. F3: remove the promise; construct two instances that share the identical visible prefix (and identical bits above n) but differ in a hidden position (e.g., in one, a_i = b_i = 0; in the other, a_i = b_i = 1), which forces different optimal x and different maximal products—hence no function of only the visible prefix can be correct on both.

title: total-characters-in-string-after-transformations-i
sketch: Restrict access so the solver can peek only the first P characters of s; indices > P are unreachable. F2: Promise that every hidden character (i > P) is 'a' (or, equivalently, provide the exact multiset/counts of letters in the hidden suffix). Then the answer is computable from the visible prefix plus (n−P)*len_after_t('a') mod M. F3: With no promise about the hidden part, take two inputs sharing the same first P characters but with s_{P+1} = 'a' vs 'z' (others equal); for t ≥ 1, len_after_t('a') ≠ len_after_t('z'), so the true outputs differ despite identical visible prefixes—certifying impossibility under the restricted view.

title: find-beautiful-indices-in-the-given-array-i
sketch: Restrict access to s so the algorithm can only peek positions in a visible prefix [0..L-1]; it must still output all beautiful indices for the full string. F2: Promise that the hidden suffix [L..n-1] contains no start of a and no start of b (i.e., all occurrences of a and b lie in the visible prefix), so every i’s beauty status is determined entirely by the visible part. F3: With no promise, take a prefix where a occurs at some i near the boundary and there is no b within k to the left; construct two completions sharing that prefix: one places a b at some j in [i, i+k] in the hidden suffix, the other has no such b (or even has an a in the suffix), yielding different true outputs for the same visible prefix, proving impossibility.

title: maximum-number-of-jumps-to-reach-the-last-index
sketch: Restrict access so the solver can peek only within a visible prefix of nums; indices ≥ m are hidden/inaccessible. F2: Guarantee the hidden suffix is a ladder: (i) for the first hidden index m, |nums[m]−nums[i]| ≤ target for every visible i<m, and (ii) for all j≥m, |nums[j+1]−nums[j]| ≤ target; then the answer is determinable from the prefix as max_jumps_within_prefix + (n−m). F3: Without any guarantee, construct two completions sharing the same visible prefix—one where nums[m] is within target of nums[m−1] and the suffix is a ladder (yielding a finite maximum), and another where nums[m] is set far so no visible i can reach any hidden index (making n−1 unreachable and the answer −1)—showing impossibility for any prefix-only view.

title: count-zero-request-servers
sketch: Restrict the solver to a sliding-window interface over logs sorted by time: it may peek which boundary crossing (left-expire or right-include) is next for the current target query, and has exactly one state-changing op advance(), which consumes one boundary crossing (toggle inclusion of one log) and updates per-server in-window counts and the active-server tally. F2: require processing queries in nondecreasing time; set the budget to the exact number of boundary crossings needed to reach all target windows (size of the first window plus the sum over consecutive queries of the symmetric difference of their log sets), which is tight since each advance() can change window membership by at most one log. F3: set the budget to that minus one; this is infeasible because at some step a target window differs by k>0 logs from the current window, and with at most k−1 advance() calls you cannot reach the exact membership, certifiably forcing at least a ±1 error in the zero-request count for that (or a later) query.

title: longest-subsequence-with-decreasing-adjacent-difference
sketch: Add an extra semantic requirement: the valid subsequence must include certain specified indices as consecutive elements in a given order. F2: choose one or more such anchored triples (or pairs) (i<j<k) whose precomputed adjacent diffs satisfy |nums[j]-nums[i]| >= |nums[k]-nums[j]|, so the constraint is compatible and still feasible. F3: inject a triple (i<j<k) with |nums[j]-nums[i]| < |nums[k]-nums[j]| and require them to be consecutive in the subsequence; this forces an increase in adjacent differences and thus makes the task impossible, with the certificate being the indices and the shown inequality.

title: minimize-length-of-array-using-operations
sketch: Restrict the solver to a workspace with peek(i) and a single state-changing operation combine(i,j) (only allowed when both entries are >0) that deletes i and j and appends nums[i] % nums[j]; count only combine calls against the budget. F2: set the budget K to n - L*, where L* is the true minimum achievable length for the given input; this is tight because each combine reduces the length by exactly 1, and an optimal sequence uses exactly K combines to reach length L*. F3: set K = n - L* - 1 for that same input (e.g., nums = [5,5,5,10,5] has L* = 2, n = 5, so K = 2); infeasibility is certified by the invariant that starting from length n you need at least n - L* combines to ever reach length L*, so with K one less than that, it is impossible regardless of strategy.

title: maximum-subarray-sum-with-length-divisible-by-k
sketch: F2: Single-pass stream with a RegisterBank of R = k + 2 64-bit registers; maintain S = running prefix sum (1 reg), best = current maximum answer (1 reg), and Min[r] = minimum prefix sum seen for each residue class r in [0..k-1] (k regs). On each next() update S, let r = i mod k, update best = max(best, S - Min[r]), and Min[r] = min(Min[r], S). F3: Reduce to R = k + 1 (or fewer) registers; then two residue classes must share state (pigeonhole), so an adversary can craft two inputs that yield identical machine state up to some point but whose true optimum later depends on choosing the lower of those two classes’ distinct minima, giving different correct outputs—hence no algorithm using ≤ k + 1 registers can be correct on all inputs.

title: minimum-number-of-changes-to-make-binary-string-beautiful
sketch: Use an interface with peek(i) and a single state-changing op set_bit(i, b). Let M be the number of disjoint adjacent index pairs (2k, 2k+1) where s[2k] != s[2k+1]. F2: cap set_bit calls at M; this is tight because any beautiful string must have s[2k] == s[2k+1] for all k (even-length blocks align with these pairs), and we can fix each bad pair with one change. F3: cap at M-1; impossible, since each set_bit can fix at most one bad pair and every bad pair requires at least one change, so fewer than M changes cannot satisfy the necessary pair-equality condition.

title: count-of-substrings-containing-every-vowel-and-k-consonants-i
sketch: F2: Single-pass stream.next_char() with a fixed RegisterBank whose total capacity can hold the last index of each vowel (5·ceil(log2 n) bits) plus either a counter or the index of the (k+1)-th most recent consonant; this suffices to update, at each step, how many starts yield substrings ending here that include all vowels and have exactly k consonants, accumulating the answer. F3: Reduce total register capacity to below 5·ceil(log2 n) bits so the machine cannot uniquely encode the 5-tuple of last vowel positions; by pigeonhole there exist two prefixes over vowels with different 5-tuples mapping to the same state, and with k=0 (and e.g., no further suffix or a consonant-only suffix) these yield different correct totals, so any such limited-memory solver must err.

title: split-array-into-maximum-number-of-subarrays
sketch: Restrict access so the solver can only peek the first P elements; the suffix is hidden and unreachable. F2: add a guarantee that every hidden element equals the running AND after the visible prefix (or at least has 1s in all bit positions that are 1 in that running AND), so the overall AND and the number of zero-crossings (hence the maximal segment count) are fully determined by the visible prefix. F3: with no suffix guarantee, two arrays sharing the same visible prefix can force different true answers, e.g., prefix [1] followed by suffix A = [1,1,1] gives total AND > 0 so answer = 1, while suffix B = [0,0,0] yields total AND = 0 and allows 3 zero-AND segments; thus no function of the visible prefix alone can be correct for all inputs.

title: count-beautiful-substrings-i
sketch: Use a single-pass stream.next_char() with only a RegisterBank as memory; maintain prefix delta = (#vowels − #consonants) and note the condition reduces to counting pairs (i<j) with equal delta and (j−i) multiple of M = 2*m, where m is the smallest integer with m^2 divisible by k (so bucket by (delta, i mod M)). F2: provision exactly enough register capacity to store a histogram counter for every bucket that can appear for length n, i.e., (2n+1)*M counters each large enough to count up to n (ceil(log2(n+1)) bits), enabling a correct one-pass update-and-accumulate solution. F3: shrink total capacity below this bound (even by 1 bit), so by pigeonhole two distinct histograms—and thus two inputs with different true answers—map to the same register state, certifying impossibility under the single-pass/RegisterBank model.

title: minimum-deletions-to-make-string-k-special
sketch: Treat the input as a single-pass stream of characters with access only to a fixed RegisterBank. F2: allow exactly 26 registers (one per lowercase letter), each with ceil(log2(n+1)) bits where n = |word|, and only registers.get/set while streaming; this suffices to maintain exact per-letter counts and then compute the minimum deletions for the given k. F3: reduce total capacity below what’s needed to represent all 26-tuples of counts summing to n (e.g., fewer than 26·ceil(log2(n+1)) bits); by pigeonhole, two distinct histograms must collide—concretely for k=0, histograms H1 = [t,t,0,...] and H2 = [t+1,t-1,0,...] yield different optimal deletions (0 vs 2), yet a colliding register state would force the same output, proving impossibility.

title: apps_4604
sketch: Restrict access so the solver can only peek the first L entries of A; the remainder of A is hidden/unreachable. F2: Provide a guarantee about the hidden suffix that the overall multiset of A-values exactly matches the position-difference multiset for N (i.e., for N odd: one 0 and two of each even in [2..N-1]; for N even: two of each odd in [1..N-1]). Under this promise, the answer is determinable from N alone as 2^{floor(N/2)}. F3: With no such guarantee, choose a visible prefix that doesn’t yet violate counts and admit two completions with identical prefix but different answers; e.g., N=5 and prefix [2,4,4,0], completion with suffix [2] yields a valid multiset (answer 4), while suffix [0] violates counts (answer 0). Since both share the same visible part, no function of only the visible prefix can be correct on both, proving impossibility.

title: apps_4443
sketch: Add an extra semantic restriction on the output letter. F2: require that the output belong to a provided whitelist W; choose W so it contains the true successor of the given input (feasible but constrained). F3: choose W that excludes the true successor (e.g., input 'a' with W={'c','d'}), giving a certificate of infeasibility since the unique correct output is 'b' which is not allowed.

title: apps_4534
sketch: Restrict the solver to a workspace exposing only: peek_row(i) to read the current Pascal row entry and a single state-changing operation next_row() that deterministically advances [1] (row 0) to the next row via Pascal’s rule. F2: budget exactly k calls to next_row(); starting from row 0, k advances reach row k, which is tight because each call increases the row index by at most 1. F3: budget k-1 calls; impossible since from row 0, after at most k-1 advances you can only reach row k-1, so the kth row is unreachable (certificate: monotone row-index increase per operation).

title: apps_4570
sketch: Augment the semantics: the program must output the minimum fee AND certify that the chosen plan is strictly cheaper than the other (i.e., the minimum is unique). F2: add a promise that A×N ≠ B, so one plan is strictly cheaper; the solver outputs min(A×N, B) and the identity of the strictly cheaper plan, satisfying the extra rule. F3: give an instance with A×N = B (e.g., N=4, A=5, B=20); then both fees are equal, so no output can be both the true minimum and strictly cheaper than the alternative, making the requirements contradictory.

title: apps_4555
sketch: Restrict access so the agent can see only A and B; K is hidden. F2: add the guarantee K ≥ (B−A+1), which makes the answer determinable from A and B alone because the K-smallest ∪ K-largest equals the entire interval [A,B]. F3: remove that guarantee; with the same visible (A,B) but different hidden K (e.g., A=3,B=8 with K=1 vs K=2) the required outputs differ, proving impossibility from the visible part alone.

title: apps_4424
sketch: This is a simple scalar threshold check (500*K >= X) with no natural multi-step computation, workspace, or partial-information structure. Imposing operation budgets (C2), memory/register limits (C3), or prefix-only visibility (C4) would be artificial, and there’s no inherent secondary semantic requirement to leverage for C1. Therefore it doesn’t cleanly support any of the four constraint families without contrivance.

title: apps_4658
sketch: Frame it as: read the 32 input bits via a single-pass stream.next_bit(), and you may only use a fixed-size RegisterBank as working memory, then output the bits in reverse at the end. F2: total register capacity is exactly 32 bits (e.g., 32×1-bit or 4×8-bit registers), which is feasible by storing all bits then emitting them in reverse order. F3: total capacity < 32 bits; this is impossible by pigeonhole/information theory—there are 2^32 possible inputs but fewer internal states, so two distinct inputs must collide; since their reversed outputs differ (e.g., inputs differing at position i yield outputs differing at position 31−i), no algorithm using <32 bits of memory can always produce the correct reversal.

title: apps_4465
